newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Front-end Eurodollar vols under pressure.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Front-end Eurodollar vols under pressure.

text.p: Implied volatilities for Eurodollar options were under pressure as underlying futures, particularly the front months, were stagnant despite a healthy rally in the bond market, traders said.

"Many people are becoming more comfortable with the notion that U.S. monetary policy is going to be relatively steady for the foreseeable future," said John Nyhoff, chief economist of Mitsubishi Financial Futures Inc.
"Implied volatility (in Eurodollar options) has suffered additional decline on top of the relatively large decline that has come both yesterday and Friday," he added.
Implied volatility for March Eurodollar futures options stood a touch below Monday's close at 12.3/12.6 percent, while June was off about half a point at 16.0/16.1 percent.

March futures hovered a few basis points above Monday's close for most of the day, gravitating toward 94.50 -- at par with the cash three-month Euro-deposit rate. By contrast, December Treasury bond futures had risen more than a full point to a high of 114-2/32 earlier in the day.
Traders expected any Eurodollar futures contract to find difficulty climbing much above 94.50 in the near term and that December and March were already around that level.
Nyhoff added that the at-the-money straddle for December Eurodollars, which still have nearly six weeks before expiration, was offered at only nine basis points.
"That's a pretty good indication no one anticipates that the three-month Eurodollar rate and/or the Fed Fund target rate is going to be changing much over the next six weeks," he said.
At the longer end of the yield curve, implied volatilities for Treasury bond options were a touch softer after the rally in the underlying market.

"You see a little bit better buying further out in the Eurodollar curve because I don't think it has necessarily reached the neutral pricing levels," said Doug Hopkins, CME floor manager for Aubrey G Lanston.
But even potential gains in those back months were likely to be gradual and limited, providing little incentive to bid up volatilities, he added.

"What you see is a variety of traders, either from a speculative or even from a hedge standpoint, starting to peg where the market is going to settle out," Mitsubishi's Nyhoff said. "They tend to establish short volatility positions in the vicinity of the targeted settlement levels."
Traders said the market's strength, despite the Treasury's quarterly refunding this week and U.S. elections today, showed the bond market was on a bullish trend.
But they added that perception that a correction was overdue, especially with an auction of $10 billion in 30-year bonds set for Thursday, underpinned option volatilities.
Implied volatility for March T-bond futures options was off 0.1 point to around 9.85 percent.
